Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: There is a lot of confusion around this. Names in sign languages are basically nicknames. They're very idiosyncratic. There's no formal mechanism to issue them. If you're in an ASL community, people will look at your face, your body, your clothes, your behaviour, your personality, and come up with a sign that they think describes you. So, for example, I'm very tall. I'm 6'5" or 6'6". So people sign my name as TALL. Or my face is very long, so some people sign my name as LONG FACE. So it's just describing something about you. And in order to get a name, you need to be in the community and you need to be a deaf person. So, if you're a hearing person, you're not going to get a name. You're going to just sign HEARING. Or you'll sign your English name.

Question: How do names work in sign language?
items.raw: So basically, there's two types. There are descriptive ones, and then there are arbitrary. Descriptive ones are usually for people who are very well known, like say, Trump, or Obama. And you just use the descriptive, so, Trump, he has the big hair and the mustache, so that's his name. And Obama, he has the big ear, so that's his name. And then for people who aren't very well known, or even for people who are well known but don't have a descriptive sign, they're given arbitrary names. And those are usually derived from your initial, so, if your name is Sarah, you'll get a name, maybe a S name, and a lot of people have the same S name. And then the other thing that's very interesting is that names are basically trademarked. So, if someone gives you a name and you use it, and then someone else gives you a name, you can't really use it. It's like, oh, no, no, that's someone else's name. So, you really do have to really be careful.

items.raw: Sign language has its own way of making names. It's not just the fingerspelling of English names. It's the name sign, and the name sign is a unique symbol for that person, and it's mutually agreed upon. So you're not just going to make up a name sign for someone. Question: How do the mammals of the ocean hydrate themselves.
items.raw:
Hi Tom,

Thanks for your question, it’s interesting. And well, it’s very different to us, or to terrestrial mammals. So, the issue is, they can’t really access fresh water. They live in salt water. And, in fact, if they just drank the sea, they’d dehydrate. And, that’s because there’s lots of salt in there. So, in reality, they get all their water from their food. They eat things like fish and crustaceans and other mammals and all that. And, so, the water is in there. They get it from eating. And, in order to compensate for the salt in the sea, they’ve got very efficient kidneys. And, they’ve got very efficient salt glands. And, in particular, the seals, they’ve got a very efficient salt gland at the front of the eyes. So, they can secrete lots of salt. And, in fact, you’ll see it coming out of their eyes. That’s a very efficient salt gland. And, so, in summary, they get all their water from their food, and they’ve got very efficient mechanisms for getting rid of the salt. But, in the end, they’re really very similar to terrestrial mammals. It’s just that they get all their water from their food.

Cheers,

Steve

It's like the foam that's inside a marshmallow. That's what popcorn is. It's just starch foam. So, the pressure has to be high enough that it breaks the hull. And the starch is good enough to make it foam up. So, it's just, like, a little pressure cooker, and it's really a simple process. But it's just, like, really interesting. At 3:12 every Thursday morning, Mara found the book in the bread rack.

It was always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She would set it on the flour bin, wipe butter from the cover, and mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, the errands and heat and sleep would swallow the thought.

Then, next Thursday, there it would be again, tucked between cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed with the proofing cabinet and the old radio’s static. Rain pressed silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.

A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons.

She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

Mara turned to page 47. A grey heron stood in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture, in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour from her apron, unlocked the front door, and turned on the little OPEN sign.

A simple rain gauge measures rainfall by catching precipitation in a funnel and directing it into a cylindrical measuring tube. 

To ensure accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner measuring tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. For example, if the collection opening has ten times the area of the inner tube, one inch of rainfall will fill the tube to a height of ten inches. This magnification allows observers to easily and precisely read very small amounts of rainfall, such as hundredths of an inch.

However, these instruments are subject to errors. One common source of inaccuracy is evaporation; collected water can quickly evaporate before it is measured, especially in warm or windy weather. Another major source is wind exposure. Strong winds can create turbulence around the gauge's mouth, carrying raindrops over the opening and causing the instrument to underestimate the actual rainfall.

Question: What's the difference between tornadoes, hurricanes, cyclones, typhoons etc?
items.raw: Tornadoes are essentially a very localized, low-level atmospheric phenomenon. It's a rotating column of air that's extending from a thunderstorm down to the ground, and that's the definition. And tornadoes can occur anywhere. Tornadoes can occur in Africa. Tornadoes can occur in the Caribbean. Tornadoes can occur in the UK, all sorts of places. Whereas hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones, all of these things are actually one and the same thing. They're all tropical cyclones. So a tropical cyclone is a large, rotating, low pressure system that's drawing in air, drawing in moisture from the ocean. That air rises, it cools, it condenses, it rains, and it just rotates and rotates and rotates. And it's rotating because of the Coriolis effect. So the Coriolis effect is the way the Earth rotates. As the Earth rotates, everything on Earth is rotating with it. So, as the air rises, it's pulled down towards the center of the low pressure system, and it's just rotating, and it keeps rotating and rotating. So that's what we call a tropical cyclone. A hurricane is a tropical cyclone in the North Atlantic and the Eastern Pacific. A typhoon is a tropical cyclone in the Western Pacific. A cyclone is just any tropical cyclone, so in the Indian Ocean, they call it a cyclone. But all of these things are one and the same thing. So, if I'm in the Gulf of Mexico, and I see a hurricane, and it crosses over into the Caribbean and into the Atlantic, it's the same hurricane, it's just a hurricane, it's just a tropical cyclone. If it's in the Western Pacific, if it's in the Western North Pacific, then it's a typhoon. So it's just naming conventions. We name the hurricanes and the typhoons. We have names for them. And it's just a way to track them. So, as a hurricane approaches, as a typhoon approaches, we know exactly where it is. We know exactly where it's going, and we know the strength of it. So we can get a lot of information out of these things. But tornadoes are a much different beast. They're very localized. They're very short-lived. They only last, on average, like 5, 10 minutes. Whereas a hurricane can last a week, two weeks, three weeks. And it's just, it's just different.
